title: Pre-OS Boot: ROMMONkit
summary: ROMMONkit is the Pre-OS Boot sub-technique that abuses the ROM Monitor, the boot loader firmware on many Cisco network devices, by loading an unauthorised image that contains attacker code. Where the parent category covers pre boot persistence across platforms and System Firmware covers computer mainboards, this sub-technique targets the loader that prepares a router or switch after power on or reset, so the implant sits below the device operating system and below the configuration a defender can read. The usual pattern is to upgrade the monitor image locally over a console connection or remotely through a file transfer service, then restart the device so the modified image replaces the original and becomes the code that starts the hardware. The result is persistent access that can modify device configuration, survive reinstallation of the device operating system, add capabilities that normal configuration review does not show, and remain difficult to detect because the device reports itself as healthy. Evidence is mostly version and boot behaviour oriented: unexpected monitor version strings, an image loaded from an unknown server, unusual boot or transfer activity in device logs or a file transfer service, and configuration differences that no change record explains. Because the loader is rarely updated in normal operations, any unplanned change to it deserves investigation and, where possible, reflashing from trusted vendor media under direct control.

beginner.definition: Many network devices have a small firmware program called the ROM Monitor, or ROMMON. It prepares the hardware before the device operating system starts. This sub-technique is an attacker replacing that program with their own version.
beginner.whyItMatters: Routers and switches carry all your traffic. Code at this level can change how the device behaves without appearing in its settings. It can also survive a reinstall of the device operating system. Standard device checks may report everything as normal.
howItWorks: The parent topic is pre boot attacks in general. This sub-technique targets the boot firmware of network devices, not computers.
The attacker first gains access to the device, usually through a weak password or an old, unpatched version.
They send a new monitor image to the device, either from a nearby console cable or over a file transfer service.
A file transfer service is a simple way to move files across a network without logging in to a web page.
They restart the device so the new image is written over the old one and used at the next start.
After that the device still works, but the hidden code can change settings or keep a way in for the attacker.
beginner.example: Think of a train station where the platform signs are painted over at night. Trains still run and passengers still board, and the timetable in the office looks correct. Only the signs at the platform send people to the wrong track, and nobody in the office can see them.
takeaways: Treat network device firmware as a monitored asset, and record the approved version for every model.
Alert on boot image transfers and monitor upgrades that no change record explains.
Restrict who can reach the device console and its file transfer service, because both are used for this attack.

objectives: Explain what the ROM Monitor is and when it runs on a network device.
State how this sub-technique differs from the parent Pre-OS Boot category and from computer firmware attacks.
Describe how an unauthorised boot image is delivered and made active through a restart.
Identify device logs and version checks that can reveal a changed boot image.
Explain why reinstalling the device operating system does not remove a compromised boot loader.
